ACT NOW is a community advocacy organisation that campaigns for a 'gutpela sindaun blong olgeta' - a just and equitable society.

ACT NOW Limited PO Box 5218, Boroko, NCD Papua New Guinea Phone: +675 7715 9197 Email: [email protected]

Research reports, posters, policy briefs, books and brochures

The latest annual report from ACT NOW! on the performance of District Development Authorities. The report is based on an analysis of the data published on the DDA Watch website from June 2025 - June 2026. The report reveals ongoing widespread failures in transparency, governance, and financial accountability among all 96 DDAs.

Update report from ACT NOW! and Jubilee Australia Research Centre on the Wammy Rural Development Project in West Sepik Province. The report reveals ongoing abuses of the Forest Clearing Authority logging permit.

Report published by ACT NOW! and Jubilee Australia Research Centre provides an update on the Mengen Integrated Agriculture Project in East New Britain Province.

A new investigation by ACT NOW! and Jubilee Australia Research Centre reveals that logging has continued unabated in the Wasu Forest Clearing Authority (FCA) area in the Tewae Siassi District of Morobe Province, despite serious concerns raised two years ago about the legality of the operation.

Investigation into the Eiwa Integrated Agro-Forestry Project reveals how ecologically and culturally significant tropical forest in Papua New Guinea’s Western Province is being unlawfully logged under what appears to be a Forest Clearing Authority (FCA) licence.

This Risk Alert examines the corporate structure, operational footprint, and compliance risk environment associated with the KK Connections corporate group, a Malaysian-owned forestry operator active primarily in East New Britain Province, Papua New Guinea. It forms part of ACT NOW!’s ongoing programme to support risk-based monitoring of forestry-sector participants operating within Papua New Guinea.

Customary land is the foundation on which Papua New Guinea must build its future development

Customary land is a gift we look after for future generations

Customary land economically, socially and spiritually sustains communities

Papua New Guinea must move from a model of development based on resource extraction to the inclusive model based on personal development that is envisioned in our Constitution

A 24-page booklet explaining the values and importance of customary land - buy hard copies in our online shop

Mandarin translation of a summary paper on the abuse of Forest Clearing Authorities to facilitate large-scale tropical forest logging in Papua New Guinea.

An investigative report published by Bruno Manser Fonds and Rimbawatch, that reveals the disturbing role of Malaysian-linked companies in local deforestation. According to its findings, 97% of PNG’s Forest Clearing Authorities (FCAs) which are being used to unlawfully log thousands of hectares of forest, are controlled by Malaysian-linked companies.

Published by ACT NOW! and Jubilee Australia, this report examines the Wanigela Tree Plantation project in Oro Province

The second annual report from ACT NOW! on the performance of District Development Authorities. The report is based on an analysis of the data published on the DDA Watch website from June 2024 - June 2025. The report reveals continued widespread failures in transparency, governance, and financial accountability among all 96 DDAs.

A summary paper on the abuse of Forest Clearing Authorities to facilitate large-scale tropical forest logging in Papua New Guinea.

Report by ACT NOW! on the performance of District Development Authorities based on an analysis of the data published on the DDA Watch website from June 2023 - June 2024. The report reveals widespread failures in transparency, governance, and financial accountability among all 93 DDAs. DDA Watch is an independent, politically neutral platform developed by ACT NOW! to provide the public with information on their local DDA and access to critical documents.

Kastom, Property and Ideology looks at the relationship between customary land tenure and ‘modern’ concepts of land privatisation and 'land grabbing' in Papua New Guinea and Melanesia. First published in 2017 by the Australian National University.

In Papua New Guinea powerful interests have their eyes on land. At stake are the livelihoods of most of the country's population, mostly in rural areas. This book argues that notions of 'economy' and 'development' have no meaning without a broad and inclusive focus on their livelihoods. It takes apart 'modernist' myths, such as the claim that large scale monocultures are more productive than small farming, and that customary land must be registered or 'mobilised' to provide real benefits. A Tok Pisin translation of a condensed version of the book Land and Livelihoods in Papua New Guinea

Briefing paper on the Loani Bwanabwana forest clearing project.

The third in a series of investigative reports into the abuse of Forest Clearance Authorities This case study looks at the Wasu Cattle Farm project in Morobe Province and raises serious questions about the project’s legality.

Written by Dr Hannah Harris from Macquarie University in Australia, the report examines how novel criminal law tools can be used to combat illegal logging and forest crime in PNG and the wider Asia Pacific region and how laws designed to target economic crimes (money-laundering, corruption, tax evasion) can also be leveraged in the fight against environmental crimes.

Chinese translation of ACT NOW's Timber Legality Risk Assessment, 2023. The assessment finds there is a very high risk that almost all logging taking place in natural forest areas in Papua New Guinea is illegal. The assessment is based on a comprehensive review of all the available literature, including the reports of official government inquiries, court cases, international organisations and civil society groups.

Anti-Money Laundering Risk Alert documents the body of evidence linking Malaysian logging conglomerate, Giant Kingdom Group, to forestry crime in Papua New Guinea. The report also documents a significant number of financial and designated non-financial businesses and professions in Malaysia which have significant exposure to the group.

The second in a series of investigative reports into the misuse of Forest Clearing Authorities as a cover for a large-scale selective logging operations. This case study looks at the Mengen FCA in East New Britain Province.

The assessment is based on a comprehensive review of all the available literature, including the reports of official government inquiries, court cases, international organisations and civil society groups.

item.title: Fifty years on: what PNG’s Constitution actually demands of its leaders, and how citizens can hold them to it
item.description: By Auna Melo | Independent Blog | Duncan Gabi | 25th September 2026 Fifty years on: what PNG’s Constitution actually demands of its leaders, and how citizens can hold them to it
item.content:encoded:
By Auna Melo | Independent Blog | Duncan Gabi | 25th September 2026

Fifty years on: what PNG’s Constitution actually demands of its leaders, and how citizens can hold them to it

When Papua New Guinea’s Constitutional Planning Committee reported in 1974, it wanted the country’s founding document to do something unusual: function not just as a rulebook for government structure, but as a public “yardstick against which government performance can be judged.” Reading the Constitution that was actually adopted the following year, alongside the Leadership Code and the Organic Law on the Ombudsman Commission that give it teeth, shows how far the drafters went to turn that ambition into enforceable machinery.

A standard written into the Preamble itself

The Constitution’s National Goals and Directive Principles, carried over almost word for word from the CPC’s draft, open by declaring integral human development as the first goal: that “every person” be freed “from every form of domination or oppression so that each man or woman will have the opportunity to develop as a whole person in relationship with others.” The third goal is explicit about leaders specifically, calling for “our leaders to be committed to these National Goals and Directive Principles, to ensure that their freedom to make decisions is not restricted by obligations to or relationship with others, and to make all of their decisions in the national interest.”

That phrase, freedom from “obligations to or relationship with others,” is the constitutional seed of everything that follows in the Leadership Code. The drafters were not just hoping leaders would act with integrity; they wrote a definition of compromised leadership into the nation’s founding text.

Section 27: the general duty, and what it actually prohibits

Division III.2 of the Constitution, the Leadership Code, applies to a strikingly wide range of office holders: the Prime Minister and Ministers, all MPs, provincial and local level government members, constitutional office holders, heads of government departments and statutory authorities, the Police Commissioner, the Defence Force Commander, ambassadors, and even the personal staff of the Governor General and Ministers.

Section 27 sets the general standard. A leader must not:

Critically, this duty extends beyond the leader personally. Section 27(3) requires leaders to ensure their spouse, children, and “any other persons for whom he is responsible… including nominees, trustees and agents” don’t conduct themselves in ways that cast doubt on the leader’s compliance, and if they do, the leader has a positive duty to “publicly disassociate himself” from that conduct.

Breach of any of this is defined in the Constitution itself as “misconduct in office,” a specific legal category, not a political metaphor.

The Organic Law: turning principle into itemised prohibition

If the Constitution sets the standard, the Organic Law on the Duties and Responsibilities of Leadership turns it into a detailed compliance regime. Leaders must:

Section 16 closes an obvious loophole: conduct that would be misconduct if done by the leader personally is still misconduct if done “with his consent… or by his authority” through a spouse, relative, or associate.

This is where the accountability architecture becomes concrete rather than aspirational. The Ombudsman Commission, three members, constitutionally guaranteed independence from direction by “any person or authority” (s.217(5)), has the power to:

A tribunal that finds misconduct proven must recommend dismissal, unless it finds there was “no serious culpability” and the public good doesn’t require it, in which case the Constitution allows lesser penalties: a fine up to K1,000, reprimand, suspension without pay for up to three months, or salary reduction (Constitution s.28(1A); Leadership Code (Alternative Penalties) Act, s.2). Anyone dismissed for misconduct is barred from elective office, and from Governor General or provincial executive appointment, for three years (s.31).

Even the Prime Minister is not exempt: the Constitution provides specifically for a tribunal of judges to hear misconduct allegations against the office (Organic Law s.27(7)(d)), and for suspension from office pending that investigation (s.144 read with s.28).

Where the courts fit in, and where they don’t

The National Goals and Directive Principles themselves are, by design, mostly non-justiciable; section 25(1) says so explicitly. A citizen cannot sue the government simply for failing to achieve “integral human development.” But section 25(3) does something more targeted: wherever a law or an exercise of power can reasonably be read consistently with the Goals, it must be read that way. The Goals shape interpretation even where they can’t found a standalone claim.

The Leadership Code is the deliberate exception. Section 25(4) removes the non-justiciability shield entirely for the Ombudsman Commission and Leadership Code tribunals, which “shall take the National Goals and Directive Principles fully into account in all cases as appropriate.” In other words, the aspirational goals of Chapter 2 become directly operative the moment a leader’s conduct is in question.

Basic rights, by contrast, are fully enforceable in the ordinary courts from the outset (s.57); any person with “an interest… in its protection and enforcement” can bring an action, and courts can grant relief even where infringement is only reasonably probable, not yet realised.

What’s notable, reading the Constitution against the CPC Report that inspired it, is how much more machinery the final document built than the Report’s language alone suggests. The 1974 drafters worried about foreign capture of leaders and wanted “constant vigilance”; the Organic Law responds with mandatory annual disclosure, a three year post office cooling off period, and Commission administered forfeiture powers. They wanted the Goals to be a “yardstick” the public could apply; the Constitution answers with an independent Ombudsman Commission, open to complaint from any person, exempted from the general non-justiciability of the Goals specifically so it can enforce them against leaders.

Fifty years on, whether that machinery has functioned as intended, how many disclosures are actually filed and scrutinised, how tribunals have ruled, how consistently the three year lockout has been applied, is an empirical question the constitutional text alone can’t answer. But it’s worth being precise about what the drafters actually built: not a set of moral exhortations, but a specific, itemised, independently enforceable code, with named penalties and a body constitutionally shielded from political control to apply it.
